e.t: This noun refers to a willow-like tree. It is the name of a type of plant rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, it occurs ten times. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its use there, but its basic meaning remains a tree identified by its resemblance to a willow. [p03:word:lxx:L700179:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700179:occurrences]

Adōnaie, also given as “Athonee,” is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a named person or figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, both times in Judges: Judges 13:8 and Judges 16:28. The name’s specific referent and significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes someone as “gaining the prize.” It presents the person as attaining the reward or victory being sought, rather than merely striving toward it. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 3 Maccabees, but the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its exact force in either passage therefore depends on the sentence and context in which it appears.

This Greek LXX verb means “shame” or “ashamed”: it describes bringing disgrace upon someone or experiencing shame. It can express the condition of being exposed to dishonor, whether because of one’s own conduct or because others have treated someone disgracefully. The word occurs 89 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it commonly describes shame as a response to dishonor or public humiliation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “braggart”: a person who boasts about himself and presents himself as greater or more impressive than he really is. It is a noun, naming the person rather than the act of boasting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Job, Proverbs, and Habakkuk. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a boastful, self-important person.

This Greek LXX verb means “make different; change.” It describes an alteration from one condition, appearance, or state to another. As a verb, it expresses the act of changing rather than naming the changed thing. It occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including Daniel, Psalms, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being changed and the surrounding sentence.

This proper name refers to an Amalekite, a person belonging to the people called Amalek. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for both one individual and the Amalekites as a group. The word occurs six times, in six verses, from 1 Samuel through 2 Samuel. Its references include 1 Samuel 15:6 and 2 Samuel 1:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each specific use.

This adjective describes a textile such as a “double-sided rug; tapestry.” It refers to a woven covering or fabric finished on both sides, rather than naming an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel 17:28 and Proverbs 7:16. The surrounding verse text would determine the precise way the textile is being described in each passage, but the word itself points to a two-sided woven material.

“Examine” means to investigate or inspect something in order to understand it or reach a judgment. As a verb, it describes an active process of looking into a matter, rather than simply seeing or noticing it. This Greek LXX word occurs four times: once in 1 Samuel and three times in Susanna. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is the act of examination.

“Relate” means to communicate something to another person. As a verb, it describes the act of making information, words, or an account known, rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, this word appears eight times, from Leviticus through 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being related and the surrounding passage.

This verb means to threaten: to express or communicate danger, harm, or punishment toward someone. It describes a forceful warning rather than a quiet statement, and its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including passages from Genesis, Numbers, Isaiah, Nahum, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. The word can describe a person’s threatening words or an announced threat. Its basic meaning remains the act of threatening.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “look at” or “keep watch.” It describes directing one’s attention toward something, whether by observing it or remaining alert for it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, including two occurrences in Lamentations 4:17 and one in Habakkuk 2:1. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is attentive observation or watchful waiting.

This noun means “spider’s web,” the delicate network made by a spider. It refers to something associated with a spider or its web, rather than to the spider alone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its ordinary meaning remains concrete and recognizable: a fragile web spun by a spider. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used simply as a physical image or as part of a comparison.

This noun means “valor”: courageous strength shown when facing difficulty, danger, or opposition. It describes a quality a person may possess and display through brave action, rather than an action word itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 25 times, especially in 4 Maccabees, where the word’s repeated use highlights the importance of courageous character. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Aristoboulos is a personal name, also rendered “Aristovulos.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 1:10. The name’s precise significance for that individual cannot be determined from the name alone, and the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

Asabia is a personal name, also rendered “Asavia.” It identifies a named individual or individuals in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs nine times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in records found in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The available information establishes the name and its usage, but does not provide a separate meaning or definition for the name itself.

This LXX verb means “greet”: to address or receive someone with a greeting. It describes a deliberate action toward another person when meeting or welcoming them, rather than merely being present. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Exodus, Esther, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “asphalt,” a sticky, tar-like material. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Genesis. The word identifies a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. Its exact role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the material itself. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This adjective describes someone or something that is not opening the mouth. It presents a state of remaining closed at the mouth rather than speaking or opening it. The wording gives a precise physical description, while the surrounding verse would determine its particular force in context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in Wisdom 19:17. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific: the mouth is not opened.

Baithmacha is a proper name, also given as Vethmakha. It does not describe an action, quality, or object in the ordinary sense; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel, at 2 Samuel 20:14 and 20:15. Its precise reference is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a designation rather than as a general vocabulary term.

This adjective describes a person who is “heavy in spirit: indignant; sullen.” It refers to an inward disposition rather than an outward action, expressing a spirit weighed down by displeasure. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:20. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here, but its ordinary sense identifies an indignant or sullen state of spirit.

This Greek LXX verb means “violate” or “force his way.” It describes pressing past a person’s will, resistance, or proper boundary rather than acting by willing agreement. As a verb, it expresses an action imposed through force. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This proper name refers to Gabaōn, also given as Gavaon, a place named in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. The name occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 36 verses, with many occurrences in Joshua and additional occurrences in Samuel, Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies this named place.

This Greek LXX proper name refers to “Galaaditin” or “Galaathitin.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The word appears seven times in the LXX corpus, across four Old Testament verses and three Deuterocanonical verses. Its precise referent is determined by the passage in which it appears, since the name itself does not provide a broader descriptive definition.

Gedsōn is a personal name, also rendered Yethson, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or persons in genealogical and tribal records. The name occurs 29 times across 28 verses, especially in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it marks a named individual within Israel’s recorded family and community history, while the surrounding passage determines which person bearing the name is intended.

This adjective describes someone or something capable of drawing. It points to the ability to make drawn figures or pictures, rather than naming the drawing itself. As an adjective, it normally modifies a person, skill, or object associated with that ability. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 3 Maccabees 4:20. The surrounding context determines exactly what or whom it describes in that passage.

This adjective describes something made up of ten months or lasting across a period of ten months. It gives a specific time span rather than expressing a general idea about length or duration. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:2. The word itself identifies the period as ten months; the surrounding verse is needed to understand exactly what person, event, or comparison it describes there.

This verb means “bend about” or “turn about,” describing an act of changing direction or curving around. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 4:34. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on bending or turning around.

This Greek LXX verb means “bring to an end.” It describes an action that carries something toward its endpoint or conclusion. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, making it uncommon in this corpus. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being brought to completion and the surrounding sentence, while its central idea remains purposeful completion.

This Greek LXX noun means “power” or “ability”—the capacity or strength to do something. It can describe effective might, capability, or resources, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 529 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a broad term rather than a rare technical expression. Its precise force in any passage depends on what person, thing, or action is being described.

This adjective describes something that has an unpleasant smell—something ill-smelling. It functions as a descriptive word, telling the reader about the odor of a person, object, or place rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:25. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Eleale, also rendered Eleali, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or locality rather than describing an action, quality, or person’s character. The name occurs five times in the LXX, in Numbers, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its normal function is simply to designate Eleale. It should therefore be read as a place-name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

Eliōēnai, also given as Eline, is a proper name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual by name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times, in passages from 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Since no verse text or further lexical definition is available, the identity of the person in each passage must be determined from its surrounding context rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “bear”: to carry, endure, or bring something, depending on the sentence. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person or object. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 15:17. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being borne there, but its basic meaning remains the act of bearing or carrying. [p03:word:lxx:L704632:identity; p03:word:lxx:L704632:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L704632:reference:0]

“Enakim” is a proper name for a people or group named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or an action word, but a specific designation used for the Enakim. This name occurs nine times in the LXX corpus, chiefly in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and also appears in Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “act of destruction”: a deed or process by which something is completely ruined or wiped out. It names the destructive action itself rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at 1 Samuel 15:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the sentence where it appears.

This verb means “discharge at,” describing the act of sending or releasing something toward a person or place. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in four verses: three in Job and one in Ezekiel. The word’s precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an active sending or releasing directed at a target.

This adjective describes something connected with victory or marked by triumph. It presents a victorious quality rather than naming the act of winning itself. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clearly victorious or triumphal. The word therefore points to success, celebration, or honor associated with overcoming an opponent. [p03:word:lxx:L705213:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705213:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L705213:reference:0]

This word means “year”. It refers to a full period of time used when describing age, duration, service, or the passing of seasons. As a noun, it identifies a measured span within which events occur or obligations continue. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 641 times, showing that it is a regular way to speak about time across many kinds of passages. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a year as a unit for measuring earthly time.

gl: place for the training of youth
d: place for the training of youth

e.t: This noun means a place for the training of youth—a location set apart for educating and preparing young people. It refers to a facility rather than to the young people themselves or to the act of training. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning identifies an institution devoted to youth instruction and development.

Ziza is a proper name, rendered “Ziza.” It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 23:10–11 and 2 Chronicles 11:20. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further meaning beyond identifying the individual or individuals called Ziza.

This word means “sea,” referring to a large body of salt water. It is a noun used for the sea as a geographical feature and as a clearly recognized part of the created world. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 408 times, showing that this is a broad and ordinary term rather than a rare expression. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the sea or seas.

This adjective describes someone as “bold” and “of good courage”—ready to act with confidence rather than fear. It is a character word, identifying a person or people as courageous. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:13. The word’s basic meaning is therefore a clear description of courage and inner confidence, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that quality is expressed in context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to spoil or prey—the person, animal, or goods taken as the result of a hunt, capture, or victory. It names something seized rather than the act of seizing it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Leviticus, Ecclesiastes, and Jeremiah, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse. Its central idea remains what has been captured and taken possession of, whether that is understood as hunted prey or acquired spoil.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Iada” or “Iatha.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 9:42. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the person’s identity and role cannot be stated more specifically here. The two approved forms, “Iada” and “Iatha,” represent the name’s recorded renderings in this LXX entry.

Ianouou is a personal name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as the name of an individual. It is preserved in the forms “Ianouou” and “Ianuu,” rather than translated as a descriptive word. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 14:6. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the person’s role or significance cannot be stated from the name alone.

Ieremin is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 42:3. The available lexical information gives the meaning simply as “Ieremin”; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role or significance in that passage.

Iesrae, also rendered Iezrae, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word or action. It identifies a specific named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:8. Since the available record gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further here. The two forms, “Iesrae” and “Iezrae,” represent the same recorded name.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Iōazae” or “Ioazae.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its function is to identify an individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:45. The available lexical information preserves the name’s form but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of the name itself.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something that produces changes or brings about a new state. It focuses on the effect of an action, person, or thing: what it causes to become different. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:23. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the specific object or situation described there cannot be stated safely. Its central meaning remains the idea of causing change, rather than merely being different itself.

This verb means “staunch”: it describes being firm, steady, or resolute rather than giving way. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 10 times, appearing in Job and Isaiah as well as the deuterocanonical books, especially 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is steadfast endurance or determined persistence throughout.

This verb means to have compassion upon someone—to respond with mercy or pity toward that person. It describes an action rather than a person or object, expressing compassionate treatment. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:10. The available lexical meaning establishes its central sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly who receives compassion and how the action functions there.

The word means a thief—a person who takes what belongs to another without permission. It is a noun used for someone identified by this wrongful act. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, showing that the term is used across laws, wisdom writings, and prophetic material. Its basic meaning remains focused on the person who steals, while the surrounding passage determines the specific circumstances or seriousness of the theft.

This Greek LXX verb means “distribute flesh” or “divide the flesh.” It describes the action of separating flesh into portions or assigning it for distribution. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Leviticus 8:20; its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “swan,” the name of a large water bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:16. The word itself identifies the bird rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is needed to explain how the name functions in that particular setting.

This word means “rower,” a person who propels a boat or ship by using oars. It is a noun naming someone with a practical role in sea travel, rather than describing the vessel itself or the act of rowing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in Ezekiel 27, a chapter that repeatedly speaks about ships, their crews, and their maritime activity. The word therefore identifies members of a ship’s working crew whose task was to move the vessel through the water with oars.

This verb means “cast lots” or “allotted,” describing the assigning of something by lot or receiving an assigned portion. It can therefore refer either to the act of deciding by lot or to what someone receives through that decision. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is allocation by lot. [p03:word:lxx:L708052:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L708052:occurrences]

This word means “stone” and describes something connected with or characterized by stone. As an adjective, it normally modifies a noun rather than naming an object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times across 20 verses, especially in passages referring to stone tablets or other stone objects. Its ordinary sense remains concrete and material; the surrounding verse determines exactly what stone-related thing it describes.

Lysimachos is a personal name, rendered as “Lysimachos” or “Lisimakhos.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the name occurs seven times: once in Esther and six times in 2 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any individual passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding verse, but the word itself functions simply as that person’s proper name.

This noun means “mandrake,” the name of a plant mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It refers to the plant itself rather than to an action, quality, or person. The word occurs six times in the LXX, appearing in Genesis 30 and Song of Songs 7. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains the name of this plant.

gl: in the midst; in the middle
d: in the midst; in the middle

e.t: This word means “in the midst; in the middle.” It describes something positioned between other things or located at a central place. As an adjective or noun, it can identify what is between, among, or centrally situated, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 757 times, showing that this is a broad, ordinary word for location or position rather than a specialized term. Its exact English rendering depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains being in the middle or midst.

Moseri is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. Its supplied lexical definition is simply “Moseri,” so the available information identifies the name rather than explaining an additional descriptive meaning. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezra 9:1. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the specific person, group, or referent named by Moseri cannot be stated safely. Its precise reference must therefore be understood from the passage in which the name appears.

This word means “sinew,” the tough connective tissue that joins muscle to bone and helps give the body strength and movement. It is a noun naming a physical part of the body. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs six times, including descriptions of human bodily structure and strength. The word appears five times in the Old Testament portion of this corpus and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the body’s sinew or tendon.

This adverb means “carefully” or “attentively.” It describes the manner in which someone looks, listens, considers, or responds, directing attention closely rather than casually. The word therefore adds careful focus to an action without naming the action itself. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:1. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding instruction, but its ordinary meaning emphasizes alert, deliberate attention.

This noun means “destruction” or “ruin.” It refers to a state of devastation or collapse—the result in which something is ruined or destroyed, rather than an action expressed as a verb. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees. Because there is only one recorded occurrence, the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine the precise force of the word there.

This Greek LXX noun means “opening,” referring generally to an opened place, gap, or entrance. Its basic sense is concrete rather than abstract: it identifies a space through which something may be seen, entered, or accessed. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including Exodus, Ecclesiastes, Obadiah, Zechariah, 4 Maccabees, and Song of Songs. The surrounding verse determines whether the opening is described physically or used as part of an image.

Ornia is a proper name preserved as “Ornia,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical entry gives no additional definition beyond the name itself, so its meaning is its identifying function: it names someone or something called Ornia. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Samuel 3:4 and once in 1 Kings 4:5.

This adjective describes someone or something as acting contrary to law—lawless. It points to conduct that disregards lawful order rather than simply describing weakness, ignorance, or an ordinary mistake. In the Greek Old Testament and its deuterocanonical books, it occurs 60 times, so it is used broadly for people or actions characterized by opposition to law. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains behavior that violates law.

gl: fall in by the way; creep
d: fall in by the way; creep

e.t: This verb means “fall in by the way” or “creep,” describing something that enters or comes along incidentally rather than being the main focus. It is an action word, so it presents movement or arrival rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but the central idea is an unexpected or unobtrusive coming in.

This word means “father,” referring to a male parent or ancestor. As a noun, it identifies a family relationship and can describe the person from whom a child or household descends. It is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, with 1,235 occurrences, so its basic meaning is broad and well established. The surrounding passage determines whether it refers to an immediate parent, an earlier ancestor, or a father in a family relationship.

This Greek verb means “superior to others; prevail,” describing someone or something that comes out ahead or remains stronger than others. It expresses success, dominance, or victory rather than merely existing or continuing. In the LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is overcoming or being superior.

This LXX noun means “making to wander; dispersing.” It describes the act or result of causing someone or something to move away from a settled course or place. The central idea is separation through wandering or scattering, rather than simple travel. It occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, across Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, showing use in several settings without changing its basic sense.

This Greek LXX word means “full,” describing something that contains what is needed or has reached its complete measure. It can function as an adjective or as a noun, depending on how it is used in a sentence. The word occurs 116 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it commonly expresses fullness rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and subject.

This Greek LXX verb means to conduct or escort someone from one place to another. It describes the action of accompanying, guiding, or leading a person rather than merely being present. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea remains actively accompanying or leading someone.

This verb means “sit near,” describing the act of remaining close beside someone or something. It presents nearness as a physical position rather than merely an abstract relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:40. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who is sitting near whom and why, but the word itself centers on staying close or being stationed nearby.

e.h: A Woman Who Is a Prophet
e.t: This word means “prophet,” specifically referring to a woman who speaks or serves as a prophet. It is a noun used for a female prophetic figure, rather than a general word for prophecy itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in passages referring to women associated with prophetic ministry. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but the basic meaning remains a woman recognized as a prophet. The word appears in Exodus, Judges, Kings, Chronicles, and Isaiah.

Raphaia, also rendered Rhafea, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, each in a separate verse, mostly in 1 Chronicles and once in Nehemiah. Its meaning here is therefore the identification of a person named Raphaia; the surrounding verse is needed to determine which individual is intended in each occurrence.

Raphi, also rendered Rhafi, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Kings 2:46. Because names identify people rather than describe an action or quality, its meaning is chiefly its use as that person’s designation. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the individual’s role in the passage; the name itself does not carry a broader ordinary description.

Roubeni, also rendered Rhuvini, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word appears once, in 1 Chronicles 26:32. The available lexical meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise reference in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX noun means “flesh”—the bodily substance of a person or animal. It names physical flesh itself and is used as a common noun throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. The word occurs 200 times in this LXX corpus, so it is a broad, recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains flesh.
